approachQuestion.prompt:
Circular handoffs. Each directed edge u -> v means a document can be handed from team u to team v. Return true exactly when some document could follow one or more handoffs and return to the team where it started. A cycle anywhere in the graph counts, even in a disconnected region.

Input: read-only outgoing adjacency lists for teams 0 through V-1, 1 <= V <= 200000 and 0 <= E <= 400000. Edges may include self-loops, but no duplicate ordered pairs. Output: one boolean.

Example 1: lists=[[1],[2],[1],[]], output=true, using 1 -> 2 -> 1.
Example 2: lists=[[1,2],[3],[3],[]], output=false; two routes may merge without a circular handoff.
Example 3: lists=[[],[1]], output=true.

options.text: Run a DFS forest with unseen, active, and finished states. Keep explicit frames with each active vertex and its next neighbor index. An edge to an active vertex reports a cycle; mark a vertex finished only after its outgoing list is exhausted.
options.feedback: Active frames form the current directed route. An edge back into that route closes a cycle; an edge to a finished vertex alone does not. Scanning all roots catches disconnected cycles.

options.text: Compute indegrees, repeatedly remove zero-indegree vertices and decrement outgoing neighbors, and report a cycle exactly when fewer than V vertices can be removed.
options.feedback: A directed cycle cannot lose its last incoming cycle edge through zero-indegree removal. Conversely, any nonempty remaining finite graph with positive indegree everywhere contains a cycle. The queue and indegree array have the same resource bounds as the DFS forest.

options.text: Traverse the graph and report a cycle whenever an edge points to any previously visited vertex, without distinguishing active and finished vertices.
options.feedback: For lists=[[1,2],[3],[3],[]], a traversal can finish 3 through 1 and later encounter 2 -> 3. The graph is acyclic: meeting an already completed route does not close the current route.

options.text: For every vertex, run a full three-state DFS reachable from it with freshly reset states. Report true if any run finds an active-ancestor edge; otherwise return false.
options.feedback: Each run is a valid directed-cycle check, so the final answer is correct for all inputs. Resetting states for every root repeats completed work; retaining finished states across the forest avoids those repeated traversals.

feedback.reason: Directed-cycle detection needs route membership rather than a single visited bit. Both a DFS forest with active states and zero-indegree elimination solve the whole graph optimally.
details: Initialize every state as unseen. For each unseen vertex, mark it active and push a frame containing the vertex and next-neighbor index zero. Inspect the next outgoing edge of the top frame and advance that frame index. An active neighbor proves a cycle. For an unseen neighbor, mark it active and push its frame. Skip finished neighbors. When a frame has no remaining edges, mark its vertex finished and pop it. If all roots finish without an active-neighbor edge, return false.

An edge to an active ancestor closes a directed cycle; an edge to a finished vertex does not. Frames need neighbor-progress state to distinguish these statuses and finish a vertex only after its descendants.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze three-state-dfs, not indegree-elimination. V counts vertices and E directed edges. Initialize a V-entry state array and scan every root. Store each frame as a fixed-size pair of vertex ID and next-neighbor index in a preallocated stack of capacity V. Access adjacency lists directly without slicing or copying. State/index operations are constant time; no hashing, amortized growth, or recursion is used. Exclude input lists and the boolean output, but include states and frames. Consider a graph that does not return early.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard worst-case bound for the specified implementation.

options.text: O(V + E) time, O(V) auxiliary space
O(V + E) time, O(E) auxiliary space
O(V(V + E)) time, O(V) auxiliary space
O(V + E) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Three-state DFS processes every directed edge once using saved neighbor indices.
details: The option “O(V + E) time, O(V) auxiliary space” is tight: each vertex changes from unseen to active to finished once, each frame index advances across its own outgoing list once, and initializing/scanning roots costs V. The state array and reserved frame stack each use O(V) space. B misses space needed for isolated vertices when E is zero. The option “O(V(V + E)) time, O(V) auxiliary space” describes fresh searches with reset states rather than one retained DFS forest. The option “O(V + E) time, O(1) auxiliary space” omits both the state array and explicit stack; replacing recursion with frames does not remove traversal storage.
